articles.title: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
articles.summary: The appointment was made after it emerged Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman believed to be a spy for China.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boom By Kali Hays ,  Technology reporter   and   Lily Jamali ,  North America Technology correspondent 
- Published 10 November 2026 
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy. 
Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. 
Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe . 
The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday. 
Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools. 
It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race. 
Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia. 
Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked. 
Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern. 
- 
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy 
- Published 11 hours ago 
- 
Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond 
- Published 3 days ago 
According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. 
Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China". 
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him. 
However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing. 
The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary. 
When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. 
It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? 
Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce. 
Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts. 
The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company. 
He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity. 
It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang. 
A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

articles.title: What we know as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over affair allegations
articles.summary: The billionaire tech executive has left the company following reports of a second extramarital affair.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignation By Lily Jamali ,  North America Technology correspondent   and   Peter Hoskins ,  Business reporter 
- Published 9 November 2026 Updated 12 November 2026 
One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive. 
Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset. 
Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair. 
Huang admitted , external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children. 
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. 
- 
Nvidia stocks plummet in US after CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy 
How was Huang removed? 
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company. 
It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors. 
But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member. 
It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound". 
There was no mention of the accusations of adultery. 
Who will replace him? 
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO . 
It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. 
One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work. 
Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced. 
And there is also the option of Ian Buck, who runs high-performance computing at the firm. He developed the technology which allowed graphics cards to be used for other computing tasks, which enabled Nvidia to capitalise on the growth of AI. 
What we know about Huang's affairs 
A New York Times report at the weekend revealed Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials believed was a spy for Beijing. 
She had previously been photographed with him on several occasions. 
The tech giant's board of directors launched an independent external investigation on Sunday following the reports. They earlier said Huang's interactions with the woman were "not unusual or unexpected". 
Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him. 
She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. 
Image source, AFP Image caption, 
Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event 
Who is Jensen Huang? 
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the west coast of the US. 
He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. 
He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. 
Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff. 
He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. 
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. 
The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with US President Donald Trump. 
At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? 
Who is Alice Huang? 
US officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . 
She was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. 
Her company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, which the firm said had been investigated and debunked. 
However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singaporean government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. 
The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. 
It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. 
When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. 
China has rejected the spying allegations as "entirely groundless". 
-

- Published 2 days ago 
- 
Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond 
- Published 3 days ago

Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair 
- Published 2 days ago 
Why does it matter? 
Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world - so the slump in its value which followed Huang's resignation hits investors large and small. 
The firm is also at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among US lawmakers. 
Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. 
The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. 
Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. 
This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. 
He has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. 
The revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and US President Donald Trump at the White House 
What investigations are now under way? 
After news broke out about the first affair, Nvidia launched an independent investigation and hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. 
It will be led by Joon Kim, a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District who is now a litigation partner at the law firm. 
US President Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating the scandal, adding that Huang told him he had been unaware the woman he was with was a spy. 
Huang has also been asked to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees on 18 November, but has yet to say he will comply. 
What is Nvidia and how important is it? 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
There is no clear successor for Jensen Huang at Nvidia 
Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for gaming. 
Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates . 
Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch. 
He bet on AI at a time when "there were no customers for the stuff he was building", Witt told the BBC. 
Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure like Amazon, Google and Microsoft now use Nvidia chips. 
Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world. 
Who is Jensen Huang's wife? 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Lori Huang and her husband at a state dinner by Trump for his Chinese President Xi Jinping 
Jensen Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners. 
They married in 1985 and have two children, Madison and Spencer. 
Earlier this week, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. 
In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn. 
Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University. 
Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him." 
"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. 
"But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." 
Additional reporting by Tom McArthur in London, Ayeshea Perera and Tessa Wong in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

articles.title: Acquitted 'China spy' tells BBC: I was fall guy for security services but also naive
articles.summary: Thousands of messages seen by BBC show how a Chinese official sought details of sensitive political matters.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested him By Joe Pike ,  politics investigations correspondent   and   Phil Kemp ,  politics reporter 
- Published 11 November 2026 
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map". 
Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister. 
The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official. 
Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role. 
The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved. 
Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence. 
In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security. 
But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China. 
Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party. 
Image source, Chris Cash Image caption, 
Chris Cash, left, and Chris Berry met in 2018 when they were teaching in China 
With the government having previously said that Chinese spies were targeting UK officials across the political, defence and business sectors with increasingly sophisticated espionage operations, Cash believes his case was pursued as a warning to others. 
Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said he denied any wrongdoing and that he had been "unfairly subjected to a trial by media". 
He said he had provided reports to a Chinese company, which he believed had clients seeking to develop trading links with the UK, and those reports contained no classified information and relied on public sources. 
Cash returned to the UK in 2019, saying in his resignation message for his job in China that he felt "guilty sitting back and participating in a system that I am uncomfortable with". 
He later became the director of a small policy group run by China-sceptic Conservative MPs in Westminster. 
Meanwhile, Berry stayed in China writing reports for a large consultancy which, like many Chinese companies, has links to the government. 
Inside the China Spy Case 
The espionage row that rocked Westminster 
Listen on Sounds 
- 
Watch: Inside the China Spy Case on the BBC News YouTube channel , external 
UK security services alleged that information from the men's messages, sent on the encrypted messaging app Signal between January 2022 and March 2023, had been passed to people linked to the Chinese state. 
England and Wales' top prosecutor said the case had collapsed last autumn because government officials could not say China had been classed as an "enemy" at the time. 
This prompted accusations of UK political interference to placate the Chinese government. 
China has previously called the allegations of spying "pure fabrication and malicious slander". 
'A psychological game of chess' 
The most striking section of the messages handed to the BBC concerns Berry's account of his meeting in summer 2022 with a senior Chinese official who wanted to have "a more detailed co-operation". 
In voice notes Berry describes how, beforehand, work colleagues had told him the official's interest had been piqued by reports Berry had written, which included details of the UK's foreign policy approach to China. 
In the voice notes, Berry says he was initially aghast, but then decided: "I thought it would be interesting to go anyway… not really intending to do anything." 
Figure caption, 
Listen: Berry tells Cash about his invitation to meet a senior Chinese official 
Berry tells Cash he was driven to a government-owned villa in a grand compound. 
The experience "felt like a psychological game of chess" and "like a test", Berry says. 
He kept his hands under the table as tea was served: "I didn't want it to be obvious if I was nervous. I tested to see if my hands were shaking first, then drank the tea." 
Berry describes the senior Chinese official asking via an interpreter "about the situation in the UK at the moment, about the Tory leadership thing". 
At that time, Boris Johnson had just resigned as the UK's prime minister, and a Conservative leadership battle was taking place, which Liz Truss would go on to win. 
Berry says he jokingly tried to ask his host which candidate China wanted, but the interpreter did not translate his question. 
"And then the main guy just shakes my hand like it's time to go," Berry tells Cash. 
After receiving the voice notes, Cash replies via text the next day: "You, my friend, have just been elite captured" before adding: "You're in spy territory now". 
In many media reports these particular messages, previously released in a government witness statement, have been presented as a smoking gun - evidence that Cash knew his friend was passing on information to the Chinese state. 
But Cash insists it was a "tongue-in-cheek joke" because he knew his friend to be "a staunch critic of the Chinese Communist Party". 
The next morning, he made a joke about Berry spying for the UK and getting in trouble with the Chinese authorities, he says. Cash texted: "Keep him sweet… We may have a use for you yet". 
"I didn't believe he was knowingly spying on the UK through me," says Cash. "I trusted my friend… I wish I had seen the danger earlier, spotted it and cut off all contact." 
'Bigger deal than I thought' 
So who was the mystery official Berry had met? 
"I found out who this guy is," Berry text-messaged Cash a few hours later. "Bigger deal than I thought." 
Berry posted a link to the Wikipedia page of Cai Qi, who at the time was one of China's most influential politicians and is now, in effect, President Xi Jinping's chief of staff. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Berry identified Cai Qi (left) as the man he had met - a trusted aide of Chinese President Xi Jinping 
Whether Berry correctly identified his host remains unclear. He has since disputed the suggestion that he met someone as senior as Cai Qi. 
What is beyond dispute is that he believed he may have met someone highly placed within the Chinese political system. 
For Chris Cash, this unusual encounter did not prompt alarm bells. Asked why not, Cash tells the BBC: "Because I didn't think anything of the meeting, really." 
We ask Cash why his friend might have been asked to such a meeting. "Strange things happen in China... you know we would often brush shoulders with sort of quite senior members of the Chinese communist party," he tells us. 
Challenged about whether he had read the Wikipedia link at the time, Cash says he had "skimmed it", adding that it described him as a judge and a provincial-level official. "I just thought it was a weird meeting with a guy who'd taken an interest," he says. 
Six months later, Berry said in text messages that "off the record" he had it "on pretty good authority" that China was considering dropping sanctions against Tom Tugendhat, one of the Conservative MPs in the China Research Group, where Cash worked. 
Berry wrote that this would happen as long as the West "continued to show signals that they are willing to work together". 
The Chinese believed it would be "extremely embarrassing" if Tugendhat became prime minister or foreign secretary while under Chinese sanctions, Berry said. 
At the time of the meeting in summer 2022, China-sceptic Tugendhat was seen as a possible contender to succeed Boris Johnson, or become UK foreign secretary. 
He was actually appointed as security minister by Liz Truss, and Beijing lifted sanctions on him in January 2026. 
Was Cash concerned that Berry appeared to be passing information to him about Chinese foreign policy? 
Cash says he assumed Berry had heard this "through the grapevine at his company" which was doing business with the UK. 
He says he never doubted his friend's trustworthiness, to the extent he even named Berry as a reference on his application for a security pass for the Palace of Westminster. 
The pass was granted and, a fortnight before their arrests in early 2023, Cash invited Berry to Parliament for lunch. 
It was to be their final face-to-face conversation. 
'Complete shock' 
Cash was in bed at quarter to six on a March morning when he was woken by car doors being shut, he says. Within seconds, four UK counter-terrorism officers had barged into his bedroom at his parents' home in Edinburgh. 
"They told me to sit up and not touch anything and then said I was under arrest for breaching the Official Secrets Act," Cash says. 
"I was in complete shock… quivering... My mum was hysterical." 
Cash says the officers dressed him in dirty clothes he had worn that weekend, handcuffed him and marched him down to an unmarked police car. He was later driven to London. 
Chris Berry was also arrested the same day. 
It remains unclear how, when and why British security services became interested in the exchanges between the two friends. 
But they are likely to have found out far more about their relationship when Berry was stopped and questioned by counter-terror officers at Heathrow Airport. 
His laptop and phone were taken - this may have enabled his Signal chats to be downloaded. 
Berry later messaged Cash about it. 
Cash says he had not been alarmed by this: "I thought it was just standard... for a guy who'd been in China." 
As the investigation progressed, it became clear the authorities believed Cash and Berry had been involved in an informal, but dangerous, exchange of information that was "prejudicial to the safety and interests of the UK". 
The allegations were based on 6,273 messages between the pair - the same ones Cash has now shared with the BBC. Cash's solicitor has told the BBC they are genuine. 
They cover a period when Cash had joined the China Research Group (CRG), founded by Tugendhat and fellow Tory MP Alicia Kearns, and when Berry was working for a Chinese company called Strong, where part of his work involved writing political and economic reports for clients. 
According to court documents, Berry was said to have compiled 34 reports for a man linked to the Chinese state spy agency, relaying information passed on to him by Cash. Strong did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. 
The CRG's office was across the Thames from Westminster, but Cash regularly had meetings in Parliament. Cash did not have government security clearance and there is no evidence he had access to classified documents. 
Despite being thousands of miles apart, the two friends remained in close contact, often messaging daily. 
The messages reviewed by the BBC show them discussing topics including sanctions on China, the tech company Huawei, human rights, Hong Kong, Taiwan and British foreign policy. 
Cash says he used the Signal app for almost all his contacts with people in China - "more for their protection" - as he says discussing the government "could land someone… in trouble". He and Berry did not use the app's "disappearing messages" function. 
Much of the information they discussed was publicly available, says Cash - who has given the BBC a detailed spreadsheet with links and references in an attempt to prove it. 
But sometimes he did share with Berry his impressions from meetings and private discussions in Westminster. On 12 occasions in the messages, he labelled information "off the record" or "very off the record" before passing it on. 
Cash says this was "just me excitedly sharing things that I was doing with him at work". 
One message recounted views allegedly expressed in private by Britain's then-ambassador to China, Dame Caroline Wilson, during a discussion with the CRG about its work on China's influence on UK universities. 
Cash also messaged Berry sharing unverified rumours about the sex lives of two UK cabinet ministers. There is no evidence Berry passed this to his Chinese colleagues. 
Cash says he regarded such exchanges as routine political discussion. "We weren't working with classified information," he says. 
Acquitted and 'traduced' 
Cash was told by his solicitor the police investigation would blow over after six months and he would soon be able to return to normal life. 
But in September 2023 - six months after the arrests - the case became public when the Sunday Times broke the story of an unnamed "spy" who had been arrested in Parliament. 
Cash recalls travelling on a train while, around him, fellow passengers read the newspaper's front page story: "Commons 'Chinese spy' arrested". He says: "I wanted the world to eat me up." 
Within 24 hours he was named and pictured in the press, and both men were later charged with espionage. 
In September the following year, just weeks before their trial was due to begin, Cash received an unexpected call from his solicitor. 
"Are you sitting down?" he asked Cash. "They've dropped all the charges." 
His lawyers requested a court hearing for the prosecution to formally acknowledge that they would offer no evidence, but at the Old Bailey the newly-innocent Cash struggled to find anyone interested in his story. 
Image caption, 
Cash's life has changed almost beyond recognition, he says, but he is positive about the future 
At every previous court appearance he had been mobbed, but the press had not been informed about this hearing. 
Eventually his team found a lone BBC journalist. "I said my piece outside the Old Bailey. And that was a real high point. I felt that I could start to move on with my life." 
It wouldn't be that simple. 
Across the city, House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle was seething. "It is this Parliament that has been spied on," he declared. "It is MPs' offices that have been infiltrated." 
There would be days of political debate and a raucous prime minister's questions where Tory leader Kemi Badenoch would claim: "This all stinks of a cover-up." 
"I'd been acquitted by law, but then I was traduced in Parliament," Cash says. "It was almost like I was convicted in the court of public opinion again, by people who I had worked with and trusted and that felt horrible." 
Today Cash's life is almost unrecognisable. He has lost his dream job, his relationship, and his closest friend from university.

articles.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Jensen Huang, 63, has been called the 'Taylor Swift of tech' in the US By Zoe Kleinman 
Technology and AI editor 
- Published 9 November 2026 
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. 
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026. 
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect. 
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife. 
Figure caption, 
"He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang 
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models. 
"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right. 
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand. 
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them. 
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little. 
But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately. 
For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech. 
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year. 
I think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way. 
- 
Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy 
- Published 3 days ago 
- 
Could this be the end of 'Jensanity' 
- Published 3 days ago 
The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others. 
We don't know when their affair began or ended , but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work. 
China denies that she was engaged in espionage. 
Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies. 
China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest. 
Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations. 
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy. 
He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him. 
Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients. 
But can he survive? 
At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus. 
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either. 
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one. 
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out. 
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy. 
He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.

articles.title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: The share price dropped wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the value of Nvidia.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images By Archie Mitchell Business reporter 
- Published 9 November 2026 
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. 
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair. 
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China. 
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China". 
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort". 
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report , external . 
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. 
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia. 
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation. 
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week. 
Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage. 
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter. 
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk." 
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm. 
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy". 
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value. 
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting. 
But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry. 
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC. 
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993. 
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company. 
Huang's position vulnerable unlike other tech bosses 
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive. 
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him. 
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision. 
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies. 
Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future." 
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched. 
Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example. 
- 
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy 
- Published 11 hours ago 
Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold. 
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. 
But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology. 
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

articles.title: Scandal-hit Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang quits, plunging AI chipmaking giant into turmoil
articles.summary: US lawmakers now want to question him over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignation By Kali Hays ,  Technology reporter   and   Lily Jamali ,  North America Technology correspondent 
- Published 2 hours ago 
Jensen Huang has abruptly quit as chief executive of AI chipmaking giant Nvidia after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves from Silicon Valley to Capitol Hill. 
Nvidia is now under scrutiny from US lawmakers in Washington DC demanding Huang answer questions over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy. 
One of the world's most valuable companies as a result of the AI boom, Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines. 
Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, called an emergency meeting of her executive team to discuss the company's future. 
His alleged conduct not only potentially crossed professional boundaries, but has made Nvidia the target of questions from US politicians who have expressed concern about national security risks. 
Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang. 
On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive. 
Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear. 
And US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing. 
Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons, along with other Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, publicly demanded that Huang brief Congress on the matter. 
If he refuses to appear voluntarily before any committee that calls him, he could be subpoenaed, one Senate staff member told the BBC. 
Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday. 
According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company. 
Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close. 
Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort". 
One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company. 
It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said. 
Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public. 
Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared. 
Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information. 
The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures. 
Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming. 
But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data. 
Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO. 
Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires. 
He is far from the first tech titan to become embroiled in revelations of infidelity. 
Bill Gates of Microsoft and Jeff Bezos of Amazon had affairs exposed in the last decade. Both men are now divorced from their wives. 
Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia. 
Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago. 
Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector. 
Because of Nvidia's size and success in recent years, such a drop can have a direct impact on the savings accounts of ordinary Americans. 
Nvidia's value makes up about 7% of the S&P 500 index. That index is offered as a popular index fund in US retirement savings accounts. 
Those account balances rise and fall with the changes of the stock market.

Bomb squads have searched many schools but no devices have been found By Paulin Kola 
- Published 12 November 2026 
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations. 
Some 3,778 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported similar threats to one that created chaos on Wednesday - even though no explosive devices have been found. 
The government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated". Unlike a day earlier, only 77 schools were evacuated on Thursday, authorities say. 
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat. 
Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected. 
On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France. 
The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries. 
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings. 
Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan". 
Some officials say it originated in Taiwan. 
A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.

articles.summary: More than 6,000 Italian schools received a threat. Authorities in all three countries say there appears to be no risk to the public.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Xinhua via Shutterstock Image caption, 
These children had to leave their primary school in Rome as a result of one of the threats sent on Wednesday By Paul Kirby Europe digital editor 
- Published 11 November 2026 
Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities. 
In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger". 
"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook. 
Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police. 
It is unclear whether the incidents are connected. 
"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said. 
Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated. 
"Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said. 
Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected. 
The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools. 
The BBC has seen the email sent to Scottish schools which appeared to have similar wording, and also referenced the name Mikhail Andropov, although as leader of a "Red Owl" project. 
Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents involving Italian schools were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targeting flights, supermarkets and even hospitals. 
Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption. 
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

On Wednesday one Milan headteacher, Anna Bertato, told Italian media she had checked the email address of the sender online: "It was already classified as spam by a student at a university in Taiwan." 
Another Milan headteacher, Massimo Nunzio Barrella, told Adnkronos news agency that he had immediately realised the email was spam when it arrived in his inbox at 08:59 and he decided not to evacuate his school and reassured parents who phoned in. 
"The text seemed almost comical," said Barrella, "it was like a message from Martians: 'We have come to annihilate you.' I even had a bit of a laugh." 
Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, and pupils were allowed to return to class. Some parents decided to take their children home for the day, but the majority of schools in Milan did not send their pupils home. 
Some 280 school head teachers had already received threats in recent days, according to Italian reports. 
In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".

articles.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
articles.summary: Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global tech race has crumbled.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
BBC's Samira Hussain reports from Wall Street on what the fall of the tech superstar means. By Michael Race ,  Peter Hoskins   and   Lucy Hooker ,  Business reporters 
- Published 12 November 2026 
Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in the US and China alike, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation. 
The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom. 
He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into freefall this week, undone by romantic entanglements that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement. 
On Thursday, he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague. 
His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China. 
Image source, AFP 
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg. 
But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology. 
The company, which is still valued at nearly $4n (£3.02tn) despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses. 
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping. 
His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. 
Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream. 
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. 
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia. 
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia. 
The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology. 
- 
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation 
- 
Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive? 
- Published 11 hours ago 
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products. 
So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships. 
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. 
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit". 
But while the former Nvidia CEO is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said. 
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him". 
"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," Witt added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." 
First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset. 
After the revelations of the first affair, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting their family. 
Trump, as well as other leaders in the AI tech industry, initially backed Huang to continue in his role at Nvidia. The president described him as "honourable". 
But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by the announcement Huang was stepping down. 
In the aftermath of that news Trump said Huang had done "a fantastic job" and proposed Tim Cook of Apple as a suitable replacement at the head of Nvidia.
